Chest tightness in a 72-year-old six weeks after a sudden bereavement should not be attributed to grief or anxiety without medical assessment, particularly because takotsubo (“broken-heart”) cardiomyopathy can cause chest pain, breathlessness or fainting and can resemble a heart attack. If the tightness is happening now, is severe, lasts more than a few minutes, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, faintness, palpitations, or pain spreading to the arm, back or jaw, seek emergency care rather than waiting for a routine appointment. Grief is emotional, but it also activates the body’s stress systems, increasing cortisol and often heart rate, blood pressure and clotting, with the greatest heart-attack risk reported in the early days and weeks after a death. Stress-related blood-pressure responses can be substantial, and grief may worsen existing cardiovascular disease, so skipped antihypertensive tablets are a practical health risk rather than merely a sign of sadness. A clinician assessing her chest symptoms may reasonably consider an examination, blood-pressure review, medication reconciliation, an ECG, blood tests for heart injury and other causes, and possibly an echocardiogram or other cardiac imaging. Grief commonly disrupts sleep, appetite, concentration and daily routines, and poor sleep and inadequate food can further weaken her ability to manage blood pressure and medicines. In older bereaved adults, raised cortisol and an altered cortisol–DHEAS balance have been associated with reduced neutrophil function, which may make fighting some infections harder during the weeks and months after loss. Grief has also been associated with higher inflammatory markers, especially among people with more severe grief, but these findings are population-level associations and do not prove that grief alone caused an individual person’s illness. Cortisol is not simply a toxin to be suppressed, because it also participates in useful stress and anti-inflammatory responses, so the family should avoid starting hormone products, supplements or other treatments without a clinician. Arrange a prompt general-practice appointment even if the chest tightness has stopped, taking her medication list, recent blood-pressure readings, symptom timeline, sleep and food intake, and any missed doses, and ask the clinician how to restart or adjust medicines rather than changing doses yourselves. With her permission, a family member can help set up a pillbox or reminder, check that prescriptions are available, record blood-pressure readings, share meals, and accompany her to appointments while preserving her control and dignity. Offer grief counselling, a bereavement group, or a psychologist as support rather than as proof that her mourning is abnormal, and address insomnia with regular sleep and waking times, a quiet dark bedroom, and professional help if it persists. Normal grief often comes in waves, with periods in which a person can still experience interest, comfort or pleasure, whereas persistent despair, inability to function or care for herself, severe sleep disturbance, marked weight change, escalating substance use, or symptoms that worsen rather than ease deserve professional assessment. Ask directly and calmly whether she feels hopeless or has thoughts of dying or harming herself, and treat any suicidal thoughts as urgent by contacting emergency services and staying with her while help is obtained. Six weeks is far too early to label her grief “prolonged grief disorder,” which requires persistent disabling symptoms for at least a year in adults, but sudden death, older age and poor sleep are reasons to maintain follow-up rather than wait passively. Avoid assuming that physical symptoms are imaginary because they occur during mourning, that every symptom is caused by grief, that a normal grief timeline can be imposed on her, or that seeking medical and psychological support means the family is medicalizing love and loss.

Chest tightness in a 72-year-old six weeks after a sudden bereavement should not be attributed to grief or anxiety without medical assessment, particularly because takotsubo (“broken-heart”) cardiomyopathy can cause chest pain, breathlessness or fainting and can resemble a heart attack. [shard_02606_66831] [shard_01402_2476]

If the tightness is happening now, is severe, lasts more than a few minutes, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, faintness, palpitations, or pain spreading to the arm, back or jaw, seek emergency care rather than waiting for a routine appointment. [shard_02606_66831] [shard_03175_79778]

Grief is emotional, but it also activates the body’s stress systems, increasing cortisol and often heart rate, blood pressure and clotting, with the greatest heart-attack risk reported in the early days and weeks after a death. [shard_01169_7873]

Stress-related blood-pressure responses can be substantial, and grief may worsen existing cardiovascular disease, so skipped antihypertensive tablets are a practical health risk rather than merely a sign of sadness. [shard_01986_71239] [shard_01169_7873]

A clinician assessing her chest symptoms may reasonably consider an examination, blood-pressure review, medication reconciliation, an ECG, blood tests for heart injury and other causes, and possibly an echocardiogram or other cardiac imaging. [shard_02606_66831]

Grief commonly disrupts sleep, appetite, concentration and daily routines, and poor sleep and inadequate food can further weaken her ability to manage blood pressure and medicines. [shard_01169_7873] [shard_02112_50969]

In older bereaved adults, raised cortisol and an altered cortisol–DHEAS balance have been associated with reduced neutrophil function, which may make fighting some infections harder during the weeks and months after loss. [shard_04515_57074] [shard_00367_64542]

Grief has also been associated with higher inflammatory markers, especially among people with more severe grief, but these findings are population-level associations and do not prove that grief alone caused an individual person’s illness. [shard_03490_7032]

Cortisol is not simply a toxin to be suppressed, because it also participates in useful stress and anti-inflammatory responses, so the family should avoid starting hormone products, supplements or other treatments without a clinician. [shard_00367_64542]

Arrange a prompt general-practice appointment even if the chest tightness has stopped, taking her medication list, recent blood-pressure readings, symptom timeline, sleep and food intake, and any missed doses, and ask the clinician how to restart or adjust medicines rather than changing doses yourselves. [shard_01986_71239] [shard_06010_36360]

With her permission, a family member can help set up a pillbox or reminder, check that prescriptions are available, record blood-pressure readings, share meals, and accompany her to appointments while preserving her control and dignity. [shard_06010_36360]

Offer grief counselling, a bereavement group, or a psychologist as support rather than as proof that her mourning is abnormal, and address insomnia with regular sleep and waking times, a quiet dark bedroom, and professional help if it persists. [shard_02112_50969] [shard_02239_25643]

Normal grief often comes in waves, with periods in which a person can still experience interest, comfort or pleasure, whereas persistent despair, inability to function or care for herself, severe sleep disturbance, marked weight change, escalating substance use, or symptoms that worsen rather than ease deserve professional assessment. [shard_00898_78858] [shard_03406_76582] [shard_02724_77511]

Ask directly and calmly whether she feels hopeless or has thoughts of dying or harming herself, and treat any suicidal thoughts as urgent by contacting emergency services and staying with her while help is obtained. [shard_03175_79778]

Six weeks is far too early to label her grief “prolonged grief disorder,” which requires persistent disabling symptoms for at least a year in adults, but sudden death, older age and poor sleep are reasons to maintain follow-up rather than wait passively. [shard_05826_4468]

Avoid assuming that physical symptoms are imaginary because they occur during mourning, that every symptom is caused by grief, that a normal grief timeline can be imposed on her, or that seeking medical and psychological support means the family is medicalizing love and loss. [shard_03175_79778] [shard_03406_76582]
